title: Same-date and next-year tide subtraction reduced the mean tail persistence difference at two Pacific gauges in 2015-2024
abstract: We tested whether NOAA tide subtraction changes the difference between high- and low-tail next-day persistence at San Francisco and Seattle. We used 21,279 station-days from six US gauges in 2015-2024 and kept the same dates for all measures. Each site and calendar month had its own 5th and 95th percentile thresholds. The equal-site Pacific high-minus-low difference was -19.66 percentage points before correction and -7.81 points after same-date tide subtraction. The paired change was +11.85 points, with a 95% three-year block interval of +2.96 to +15.99 points after threshold refitting. Subtracting the next year's tide prediction gave a larger change of +17.82 points. The same-date-minus-next-year contrast was -5.98 points, with an interval of -12.89 to +1.23 points. Thus the smaller tail difference is not specific to the correct tide dates under this control. Low-tail persistence remained greater in the corrected Pacific mean. The test shows sensitivity to the daily measure, not a unique physical tide cause or a recovery time. Ten years, selected gauges, daily extrema, changing tail membership, and conditional block intervals limit inference. The package gives exact source hashes, daily evidence, counts, all resampling weights, code, a figure, source and rational arithmetic audits, and an exact offline repeat.

display.caption: High-minus-low next-day tail probability before and after same-date tide subtraction at six gauges, and the two-site Pacific mean with a next-year control. Intervals use three-year blocks with threshold refitting. Site intervals are unadjusted. The next-year control reduces the mean difference more than same-date subtraction.
